Author: @KilluaZoldyck-ef2xj
Content:
We're all feeling the pinch of ever-increasing subscription costs, often for services that remain stagnant or even decline in quality, a phenomenon aptly dubbed "enshittification". Yet, some companies seem to escape the same scrutiny as others. Take Netflix, for example. Despite steadily raising prices, introducing ads, and arguably diluting its content library, it largely flies under the radar. The user experience, for many, has arguably worsened, not improved, over the past 15 years.
This stands in stark contrast to companies like TeamViewer. While it might have been financially unsustainable for them to offer lifetime subscriptions without a clearer grasp of future operating costs, their perceived lack of tact in communicating with "valued customers" often draws significant ire. Yet, many other subscription services, with their colourful and creamy websites, manage to mask similar practices, allowing them to quietly extract more from our wallets. Imagine the outrage if Netflix addressed its users as "Hey customer" - it would likely spark far more anger than the frustration directed at TeamViewer.
The reality is that dark patterns are increasingly baked into the modus operandi of top companies, subtly ensuring a steady stream of revenue. The implicit understanding is that as long as enough of us continue to subscribe, these companies will remain afloat, regardless of past promises or declining service quality. Perhaps if Netflix had offered lifetime subscriptions in its early days, it could have honored them precisely because the rest of us would continue to subsidize its operations.

Author: @RamjetX
Content:
Re 3D printed files... I created a ton of parts for Sim Racing over the years. My stance on this was really simple and enabling for a seller. I didn't have the time to run a 3D printing shop. But yet it was still abused...

- You could 3D print and sell your service as a 3D printing service. But you must cite the source (my thingiverse, printables, cults etc) so that people have the option to download and print themselves for free.
- You were specifically not allowed to modify, de-brand or re-brand my models. I get nothing out of doing this stuff but the joy of helping others. De/Re branding my models robs me of a cost free thankyou.

I still see my files, on ebay, Etse and other sites rebranded as their own. I contact them and genuinely have been told to eff-off before by some sellers. 

So I stopped. I stopped sharing my files. My work was simply to give the average gamer low/no cost option to the expensive sim racing parts. And focused on helping others in the sim community how to design parts, electronics and build their projects.

Author: @Natalshadow
Content:
Another thing about "using its thoughts". There's a known cognitive problem about that. In translation we've dealt with "Machine Translation" for well over a decade now and we know that if we're provided with a machine translation before doing a translation effort ourselves, then the brain is polluted by the machine suggestion and it costs a LOT more cognitive energy to draw on creativity to generate a good translation. Your brain is basically full of shit and it costs a fortune to get rid of it.

Using AI to get inspiration is dangerous. Think first, use AI later to see if maybe you missed anything once you've exhausted your own creative output.

Author: @tadasjankevicius640
Content:
finally after 30 minutes of not understanding each other, Luke hits the 3d printing topic dead on. the issue that etsy is tackling is print farms taking publicly available 3d print files (.STLs) and selling the prints.  There is no cost for the farm to offer 10000 different products, as it is just a file on their server. the cost of manufacturing a "consumer" grade 3d print is pennies. all of the work in those products was in designing it and iterating time and time again to make it great. the printing part is cheap as dirt. All of the public STL pages have a caveat where they say it's free for personal use, it's free to re-upload a remix of the file with edits, but it is prohibited for commercial use. not like anyone cares.
The only (unrealistic) way is to license your files to print farms as sort of "approved dealerships" but that would limit the reach ridiculously. at the same time, some pages offer print services, so for example you find a thing you want and they say "hey for X amount of dollars, we will print this out for you and ship it". 
the closest example that i can think of in another market is that Leonardo designed and painted the Mona Lisa. Now, i can go and get a high quality reproduction from a licensed source, i can go to aliexpress and get a knockoff painting, or i can google the image and print it on my home printer. that's the conundrum with 3d printing licensing. it's nigh-impossible to stop unless the files are kept private.

Author: @TomDavidsonTheGreatAndPowerful
Content: The way I look at this, from an ethical standpoint: if you have paid for a perpetual license that does NOT cover full-version upgrades, then you are not morally entitled to free future upgrades. Your perpetual license gains you the right to perpetually use the specific version you paid for. Where this gets tricky is if the software requires server resources or security updates or whatever that the company can no longer support for some reason, and as a consequence the "perpetual" use of the software has a natural endpoint. I think, if this happens, the company arguably has an ethical obligation to release the source code of that version (depending on security expectations and the like). As a lifetime Plex Pass holder who's been watching how that company has been desperately trying to dance around the hole it's dug for itself with that license, I DO find myself wondering whether it's worth accepting their horrible changes to the system in exchange for keeping the servers -- without which the software is useless -- online and operational.

Content:
TeamViewer could have avoided this issue altogether. Either the security updates required a fundamental change to their existing codebase, in which case they could have used the opportunity to separate the infrastructure from the business logic and create a TeamViewer-Lite release with Version 11 features and modern security; or the security updates did *not* require a fundamental change, in which case they could have provided those updates to Version 11 through a minor update.

Author: @bradleymott7389
Content:
Dang it. I was in bed listening to WAN show to zone out when you started going down the "private equity is a bad thing" rabbit hole and I just couldn't. You've got a bad take on this, as do most these days, who say private equity firms just bilk value out of companies and let them die. Here's the thing: companies bought by PE firms are *already dying* - let's start there - in almost all instances firms bought by PE are on the way out and are bought to save the brand or company, or at least (and this is the REALLY IMPORTANT PART), *to have a chance*. 

Look at the history of the company KKR. Yes, they have ties to Blackstone and blah, blah, blah they're so bad but I worked at First Data during the acquisition. They were also responsible for Nabisco which was mentioned live. They have also, over the years, begun giving some of that equity back to employees if they survive the downsizing and restructure that HAS to happen to save a failing business. 

Now you can look at the bad examples like restaurants who almost always fail in PE restructuring - but you have to think about why - the only real asset a restaurant has is the land on which their restaurants sit. The only thing they can leverage is that land, and the likelihood of being able to turn around on restaurant margins when you're paying rent suddenly is nearly zero. Still though.... they get a chance. If the restaurants are going out of business anyway, why not leverage every asset in the attempt to keep running? 

Lastly, regarding "what is success" - survival is success. Yes, getting sold again is success - becoming profitable without going out of business and firing 100% of your employees is success. Not every PE is a good company, but not all PE are bad companies, either. They're "a chance" to save a business, that's all PE is. It's a last resort, and not always a good one - but there are good ones out there - First Data, Nabisco, TXU, and may others by KKR as just one example. CBS Sunday Morning actually did a great video about KKR, and how they're returning value to employees: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xJiugz-QPSA

Author: @fischele5790
Content:
I strongly believe that unregulated generative AI will do the same to online content creation as cheating has done to online video games. 

Right now most AI content is easily detectable by anyone who pays attention to what they are consuming. In gaming terms, this is equivalent to a spin-bot. You know you are being cheated and there is no doubt about it.

However, there will be a point where these content generation tools are so advanced that no human will be able to distinguish them from human content. And as the technology becomes better, more creators will (partially) replace human content by AI content. In gaming terms, this is closet cheating. You don't know who exactly is cheating you, but you know that a large enough percentage is cheating so now you question every single interaction for its legitimacy.

I think this mixing of human and AI content will eventually lead to an AI exhaustion where a majority of people will look for fully human content again. But by then, it will be too late. So I don't think that the decision you are making as a content creation business is "use AI now and be ahead of the curve or be left behind". It is make a principled decision now to never use AI and retain your identity, or embrace AI and become part of a machine that will eventually destroy itself.

Most of us do not want to live in the matrix, so we should decide against it now before it is too late.

Author: @JamesMcGhee
Content:
SaaS is a predatory model. Always. It turns a product into a never-ending rental under the guise of convenience. Software is a product—you should be able to buy it, own it, and use it. Period.

Yes, software often depends on services: updates, patches, maintenance, support, maybe even online infrastructure. Those are services, and they naturally come with ongoing costs. But access to those services is not ownership of the product. The license is to the software itself. That license should be perpetual—what you bought is yours.

This is exactly how we do things:
You purchase a perpetual license for our software. It’s yours, permanently. Alongside that, you can buy blocks of time where we provide service—maintenance, updates, support, whatever you need. That can be month-to-month, annual, or custom durations. You can subscribe if you want ongoing support or just buy time when you need it. Your license never expires. You just don’t get free service forever, because that costs us time and money.

This is the fair model. You’re not locked in. You’re not renting. You own what you paid for. You pay for service only when you actually need it.

And let me be absolutely clear: piracy is theft. Full stop. You might hate Adobe, you might hate SaaS (I sure do)—but stealing software doesn’t make you a freedom fighter, it makes you a thief. Condemn the model. Demand better. But don’t pretend piracy is a solution. It's just more exploitation, in the opposite direction.

Author: @CelticShaman.
Content:
I do not believe in the phrase 'if buying isn't owning then piracy isn't stealing' as it's normally used. Just because the only way to access media is to lease it or license it and never own it yourself, that does not mean you are entitled to the software. You either get it on the creators terms, or you don't get it. I say this as someone who thinks we should go back to 100%  physical media, but that being said, the situation Linus is describing changes the math to me. If you do buy software on the creators terms and they decide to pull the rug out from under you later then all bets are off as far as I'm concerned. You are entitled to what you bought and if it is EoL'd, you are entitled to some sort of compromise or refund. But the problem here I think is legislation has been behind this issue for my entire life to the point where everyone does what they feel is right. Unfortunately, not everyone agrees on what is right. 

 it's a complicated issue but my position boils down to you are not entitled to someone else's software but if you do agree to their terms and they back out on you then you're under no obligation to honor your side of the agreement anymore.

Author: @neon-kitty
Content: This may be me being pedantic but I have to disagree on people in the 1990s not enjoying/consuming media from the 1890s or earlier. Jane Austen actually wrote her novels in the 18-teens. The first Sherlock Holmes stories were published in the 1880s. Those are still being read to this day. Plenty of music from over a hundred years ago is also still popular and considered part of the cultural mainstream even today. Then there's plays, paintings,... If you limit it to just movies (or "recorded media"), you obviously have a point because it took a while for recording technologies to mature and for filmmakers to develop the sort of general feature film conventions that we're familiar with today so many films produced from the 1930s onwards will be much more "watchable" from a modern perspective than many earlier productions (though, as you say, some people may still be put off by, e.g. the poor sound quality). But if we're talking media in general, I'd say that that's a wrong statement.

Author: @annofreak
Content:
1:13:35 What Greece seems to be doing isn't actually that odd by European standards. I think the most notable thing is the relatively extreme height of the fine. The European Court of Justice already argued almost a decade ago that users of streaming services can be considered in breach of copyright laws in cases where it should have been clear to them that the service they are using is acting illegaly.
In a different case of copyright violation, namely the (illegal) selling of windows keys, German prosecutors have opened legal investigations into buyers of these keys, based on the argument the keys were so much cheaper than in the official stores. Essentially, the deal was too good to be true. Thus the buyer has to be skeptical and perform extra steps to vet the validity of the seller.
Doesn't really seem far fetched to me to apply this "to good to be true"-logic to streaming services.

Content:
24:05 
Re: old movies. 
(There really are no movies from the 1890s). 
There are a lot of good old movies (from before the 90s). One of the issues that people our age (30s-40s) have with movies before our time is that they're so darn wholesome. Even the movies that are supposed to be action movies or whatever still kinda suck because the censors wouldn't let stuff through. 

But there are certain types of movies that are still really good. Film Noir is one of them. Movies like Double Indemnity, The Maltese Falcon, Laura, The Third Man, are all excellent movies that still hold up today. Literally _no excuses._ And if you can get them in a high quality transfer to digital, they can look absolutely beautiful. (The lighting, mood, and camera work are off the charts, even better than today, where everything looks kinda flat and they're scared to have shadows and highlights. Now, everything has to be _perfectly exposed._ You can't hide monsters in the shadows anymore, because we don't have shadows).

Author: @michaeldugger8436
Content:
I feel like getting in on the "perpetual license" is one of the only respectable way to support a serious company in the early days. 

I spent money to support KSP 1 in this way long, long ago in early access. And bought the completed game again b/c I'd lost access to the original email/steam account and was super-stoked on what they'd created. Partially thanks to me investing early. 

Even Factorio, where I bought the original game in early access, once the excellent final 1.0 game was released I figure that was the versioned they'd continue to support for my registered account. And that's what they've down. Even the expansion, which added a ton of content, still saw the QoL improvements back-ported to the non-expansion version! So OG players still get 2.0+ improvements, minus the added content. (Of course I bought the expansion anyway, so I get new content and core improvements.)

It just feels so complicated with non-game types of tools ... Like if TeamViewer released V14 and had full, non-hackery Wayland support, including unattended and/or headless access to Linux hosts ... and they'd detailed the work they contributed back to the relevant projects, then I'd feel totally okay about giving them more money. But at the same time, I'd expect them to support their latest version with the significant (non-security) upgrades disabled for my account.

And had I purchased a perpetual license at those prices ... while I think it would be fair for them to negotiate a price for the new features on my account, I'd expect them to continue to honor that I'm not a software-as-a-service customer and expect to pay per-feature that I require applied to my account permanently. Rather than a SAAS, monthly payment model.
